brief.head: Two kinds of tycoon
brief.text: Industrialists can demand protection and “rule in our small pond of a fixed size”, as the Bombay Club did, Amit Varma said, or compete globally and grow. {096-C15}

brief.head: Fight it again
brief.text: Elites assumed the case for open trade was won, from the 1909 book on trade ending war to the Washington Consensus. Every generation, Amit Varma said, must fight it anew. {096-C16}

brief.head: Ships make warships
brief.text: A country with a commercial shipbuilding industry can build warships, Ajay Shah said. Demanding “Made in India” arms fails if the wider economy lacks the skills. {096-C06}

brief.head: A dirty monopoly
brief.text: Rare earths exist everywhere, Ajay Shah said. China dominates because it tolerated the pollution of making them, and it once blocked their sale to Japan. {096-S05}

brief.head: Badenoch’s homework
brief.text: Breakfast-TV anchors harangued Kemi Badenoch for not watching *Adolescence*. To understand hospitals, she replied, she need not watch *Casualty*. Amit Varma suspected the anchors had not watched it either. {096-S11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the fate of free trade
lead.head: The shopkeeper’s last stand?
body: A week after making the case for free trade, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah turned to the question in the title: is globalisation doomed?
Shah began with a choice as old as nations. There is the martial outlook, which grabs land, and the shopkeeper’s outlook, which trades its way to whatever it wants.
“Every push in favor of autarky is taking us closer to a military and a martial outlook and a way to make progress by killing people,” he said. {096-C01}

The 1930s showed how. After the Smoot-Hawley tariffs and the retaliation they provoked, world trade fell by 66 per cent. Varma said he could think of only one other thing that would do that: a world war.
## Built for a world of goods
After 1945 the GATT, a multi-country club, drove tariffs down. On manufactures in developed markets they fell from 40 per cent in 1945 to under five, as Varma had noted the week before.

It worked, Shah said, because it left out farming, because trade then meant goods, because big corporations wanted open markets, and because the West had the leverage to drag spoilers such as India along.

Every one of those pillars has since given way. Services now dominate the world’s economies, and trade rules barely reach them. “So really it’s game over,” Shah said. “You move to services. Why hanker after manufacturing?” {096-C03}
Corporations lost interest, elites thought the battle won, and after the Cold War the West cut the budgets that gave it leverage.
## The China problem

Then came China. Shah, a committed free trader, laid out four worries: selling military capability to a rival, chokepoints such as drug ingredients and rare earths, hidden subsidies that build monopolies, and a giant economy exporting its debt troubles as cheap goods.
He set himself a rule. “A person like me who is getting worried about this must explicitly articulate scenarios of harm,” he said. {096-C05}
Varma dissented. If China subsidises cheap goods, he argued, consumers save money that creates jobs elsewhere, and the subsidy should be welcomed.
## A shock to the system
Into this, Shah said, came “a stable genius called Donald Trump”, with tariffs on every country at once and rates worked out from bilateral trade deficits, which he called nonsense.

The worse damage, Shah argued, is uncertainty. Wrecking supply chains built over decades is “tantamount to throwing bombs on certain present production facilities”, a cut in the world’s capital stock. {096-C12}
The way forward, he said, is deep integration: willing countries, the rest of the OECD plus India, agreeing rules so tight that cheating is hard, with the door open to all who accept them.
Nearer at hand, he sees a deep India-US free trade agreement as feasible, and he praised the Union government’s thinking.
Varma went further. “My dream is that we have no tariffs at all,” he said. “Forget trade agreements, unilaterally remove all tariffs.” {096-C14}
Cars alone, he said, would be 30 per cent cheaper.
Shah ended on hope. “My dear friend Amit, I am optimistic that something good is coming our way.”

second.label: Economic statecraft
second.head: Bitter pills from China
second.deck: Ajay Shah on India’s drug makers and a rival’s grip on their ingredients
body: India makes good-quality generic drugs for the world, but many of their raw ingredients, called APIs, come from China. About 80 per cent of the world’s capacity for making them sits there, Ajay Shah said. {#apis}

Ideally, an Indian firm such as Dr. Reddy’s buying from a Chinese supplier would be a private deal. But Chinese firms are indirectly controlled by the Communist Party, and Shah imagined a negotiation over Ladakh in which China threatens, in private, to cut off API exports to India. {096-S04}
The daft response, he said, would be to hand one company at a time a big contract. He, Vijay Kelkar and co-authors have worked out a design that uses the state minimally and without corruption.

quote.text: When you have a vulnerability that turns into the power to threaten a government.

second.caption: the Chinese API lever

third.head: Most favoured, least loved
body: In the language of trade, “most favoured nation” is not a compliment. It is a piece of plumbing, Ajay Shah explained, built into America’s 1934 trade law.
Some in Pakistan missed the point. Shah recalled amused commentary in the Pakistani press about hawks outraged that their country treats India as its most favoured nation. {096-S02}
The rule says that if America cuts its tariff on pencils for Germany, it cuts it for everybody. That avoids a patchwork of rates, and goods sent through third countries to exploit it. {096-C02}

Amit Varma’s gloss: you treat everyone the way you treat your best friend. Since lower tariffs are better, he said, “this is a fabulous way to incentivise”. Shah called it a kicker that builds a lasting bias towards lower tariffs.

sections.label: The aftermath
sections.head: Tariffs first, armies after
sections.caption: the road from Smoot-Hawley to war
body: In 1930 Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tariffs into law, though thousands of economists and academics had urged him not to. The United States raised tariffs on the rich countries, they retaliated, and world trade fell by 66 per cent.
Amit Varma called it a trade war with the effect of a world war. Unemployment in America, he added, stayed at ten per cent throughout the decade. {#unemployment}

For Ajay Shah the road to war is direct. Shut out of trade, nations swap the shopkeeper’s outlook for the warrior’s: the Japanese invasion of 1931, Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia in 1935, the German idea of Lebensraum.
## The president’s pen

Hoover lost the election, and Roosevelt asked Congress for presidential authority on trade, granted through the RTAA of 1934. That authority, Shah said, is how Donald Trump comes to have so much power today. {096-S01}
The law rested on reciprocity: America would cut tariffs when others cut theirs. That is not Ricardian theory, Shah said. Britain ruled the waves by cutting tariffs on its own.
But the law carried a kicker. Under most-favoured-nation treatment, a cut agreed with one country applied to all, creating a steady bias towards lower tariffs everywhere. {096-C02}
~ It had little time to work. Within a few years the world was at war again, and the rethinking began only from 1944.

quote.text: Roosevelt went to the Congress and asked for presidential authority on trade, authority that persists still today.

sections.label: The GATT years
sections.head: A club that ran out of steam
sections.caption: why the GATT worked, and stopped
body: From 1944, Ajay Shah said, John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White began dreaming up the post-war world. One piece was the GATT, a multi-country club to drive trade liberalisation everywhere.

It worked partly because its designers gave up on agriculture rather than fight farm lobbies. Japan’s rice farmers, Shah said, are “a lethal lobby”, about two per cent of the population in a country making semiconductors. {096-J10}

In 1945, trade meant goods; there were no computers and no fibre-optic cables. Global corporations lobbied for open markets. And the West used military and aid leverage to coax spoilers along, India among them.
## How it unravelled

Each pillar has since cracked. In the median country, services are 67 per cent of GDP, and 71.5 per cent across the OECD, yet trade rules barely touch them. {#services} Shah would even give up a little manufacturing for sweeping free trade in services.

Corporations, their goods agenda done, lost interest. Elites assumed the battle was won. After the Cold War the West cut its military, foreign-policy and aid budgets, and lost leverage in a WTO where every country holds a veto.
“One dinky country can be a hold up,” Shah said.
~ For Amit Varma, the lesson of both episodes was that progress cannot be taken for granted.

quote.text: The West was producing that global public good all these years, and basically the West ran out of energy.

sections.label: The wrinkles
sections.head: A free trader’s four worries
sections.caption: China and the limits of free trade
body: Ajay Shah is a free trader with four worries, and a rule for himself: anyone who raises such worries must spell out concrete scenarios of harm. {096-C05}
The first is war: why sell an enemy the means to fight you? The second is the chokepoint. India’s drug makers depend on Chinese ingredients, and China is “a party that has a country”.

Third, hidden subsidies, from cheap credit to seized land, let Chinese firms dominate simple products like solar panels. Lost know-how is slow to rebuild. “Economic development is not a manual, it’s learning by doing,” Shah said. {096-C08}
Fourth, a giant economy that answers its debt overhang by flooding the world with cheap goods is exporting its unemployment.
## Varma’s disquiet
Amit Varma first steelmanned Shah’s case, stating it so well that Shah could have made it himself. {096-C17} Then he dissented, asking how Adam Smith and David Ricardo would see it.

Cheap imports may shut local factories, he said, but consumers save money, and that money creates economic activity and jobs. “If they are subsidizing us, let us take the subsidies with open arms.” {#openarms}

~ They clashed over monopolies. Varma said no firm has ever won a monopoly with low prices and then raised them without state coercion. Shah replied that a $19-trillion one-party state is a new situation. {#trillion}

quote.text: Like between India and the UK, this would never happen.

sections.label: The Trumpist case
sections.head: Not every rule is a wall
sections.caption: the Trumpist case against free trade
body: Most of what the American right writes on trade is poor, Ajay Shah said, but a column by Robert Lighthizer was the best he had read. Shah read out its core: unfair trade means subsidies, market access limits, “rigged health and safety standards”, directed banking, currency manipulation and lax environmental rules.
Amit Varma gave Europe’s GDPR as a commonly alleged non-tariff barrier, recalling J. D. Vance protesting it.
## Birthrights and barriers

Shah separated the strands. GDPR binds European and foreign firms alike. On a visit to Sahyadri Farms in Nashik, the hosts learnt that grapes bound for Europe may get no pesticides for two months before harvest. {096-S06}
French growers face the same rule, Shah said, and a democracy choosing a high safety standard is exercising its birthright.

Each country also sets its own balance on pollution, labour and taxes, so India’s lower standards are no subsidy. “You can’t take today’s Swedish standard and apply that to India,” he said. {096-C10} Carbon dioxide, a global pollutant, is the exception.

~ Real non-tariff barriers exist, he said, such as India’s data-localisation rules, which keep out good foreign cloud providers and raise costs for Indians. Some of Lighthizer’s case holds; some is “mumbo jumbo”.

quote.text: Now that’s a level playing field whether you grow grapes in France or you grow grapes in Nashik.

sections.label: The tariffs
sections.head: Eggs, deficits and bad maths
sections.caption: the Trump tariffs
body: The tariffs came on every country at once, which needed a negotiating capability that is unlikely to exist, Ajay Shah said. Then Donald Trump changed his mind: a 10 per cent tariff on everybody, and 145 or 245 per cent on China. {#tariff245}

Trump treats a bilateral trade deficit as a measure of a country’s non-tariff barriers. Shah recalled Amit Varma’s favourite illustration: Varma runs a deficit with the shop that sells him eggs, which never buys the services of a prominent podcaster. {096-J03}
The official who published the formula had an Indian name, Varma noted. “If you’re watching this, learn some math, bro,” he said. “While you’re working for Trump.” {096-J02}
## A gun to both heads
Chinese goods exports to America are about $550 billion, Shah said, some 2.8 per cent of China’s GDP. {#chinaexports} A trade war over them is “like two people holding a gun at each other’s heads”.

Shah spotted the irony. He had worried about the Chinese Communist Party cutting off goods to the world. “Well, here you’ve got the Republican Party blocking the sale of those Chinese things into America.” {096-J06}
~ The deeper damage is uncertainty: if the United States can do this, firms wonder, what might it do next? Every company planning its next factory, Shah said, has a headache.

quote.text: There is no tariff on Russia, and there are tariffs on countries that have no people.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Wanted: a new Keynes
sections.caption: deep integration and India’s chance
body: The GATT was right for 1945, Ajay Shah said, but the world now needs deep integration: willing countries agreeing rules on subsidies, directed banking, currency manipulation, intellectual property theft and carbon, so tight that cheating is hard. {096-C13}

The Trans-Pacific Partnership was conceived this way, as a WTO 2.0 with an open architecture. Shah would leave out the Chinese Communist Party and a United States losing its capability, and build the core from the rest of the OECD plus India.

Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Pakistan could join later, on take-it-or-leave-it terms. When Shah said Keynes would be dreaming of such a deal, Amit Varma replied: “In the long run, Keynes is right.” {096-J13}
## India’s moment

Short of that, Shah sees a deep India-US free trade agreement as feasible. Donald Trump could claim he had fixed fifteen ways in which India was not a good citizen of world trade; India could say it had secured a good deal.
India has already offered an olive branch, he said, scrapping the 6 per cent equalisation levy, the Google tax, “which I always thought was a dumb idea”. {096-S08}
~ After India and the US, Shah asked, why not the UK, the EU and Japan? Varma said another great opening “would please the soul of Manmohan Singh”.

quote.text: But now we are here. We’ve got many years of experience, and now we need to think of deep integration.

side.boxText: Robert Lighthizer’s *New York Times* column of 6 February 2025 was, Ajay Shah said, the best thing he had read from the American right. Several people sent it to him asking how he would respond, so he drafted a thorough rebuttal. {#column}

contQuote.text: The privilege of international trade does not come from exporting. The privilege of international trade comes from the glory of being able to buy cheap things from overseas.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Tanks, iPhones, old cars and a tearful flight: the episode’s tales

stories.start: I uh traveled to Spain recently, right? I uh flew Etihad, treated myself
stories.end: But I was just incredibly uh blown away by the power of it
stories.caption: weeping over Adolescence
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s flight from Spain, and the show that broke him
stories.head: Tears in business class
body: Amit Varma flew to Spain recently, treating himself to business class on Etihad. He loves flights, he said, because there is no internet and you can get useful work done. On the way back he watched *Adolescence* on his iPad.

Each of its four episodes is shot in one take. At first Varma thought it a gimmick. Within a couple of minutes he decided it was essential: because there are no cuts, he said, “your attention also never cuts”.

Varma recalled once recommending Krzysztof Kieślowski’s *Dekalog*, ten films for Polish television and “a web series before the web”, which he thought a pinnacle of cinema. Later *The Wire* brought a novelistic ethic to the screen. *Adolescence*, he said, is a new pinnacle.

The first half of the fourth episode undid him. “In terms of storytelling craft, in terms of the way it was shot, in terms of the acting, I have never seen something so good,” he said. He was weeping on the flight. {096-S10}
Nearby passengers looked at him as if to ask how one of the luckiest people ever could be crying. “You can have all the champagne you want,” he said, “though of course I never drink.” {096-J11}

The show had meanwhile become a political football. The right made an identity-politics point about a white boy accused of killing; others faulted it for centring the accused boy rather than the victim.
~ Varma, citing a line he attributed to Martin Amis, said the worst criticism faults an author for not writing the book you want. {096-J23} The show, he said, is about the human condition.
stories.why: Varma offered the show as proof of a golden age of culture: a masterpiece can be hugely popular, and *Anora* won the Oscar. Engaging with it, he told Ajay Shah, is engaging with the humanities. {096-C18}
stories.postscript: Shah promised to watch only episode one. “Four hours is a huge commitment,” Varma conceded. {096-J12}

stories.start: we were kind of discussing the implications of removing uh both tariff barriers
stories.end: And today luckily opening up in ninety one changed that
stories.caption: the seven-year wait for a car
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on 1980s India and the hidden price of tariffs
stories.head: Second-hand, first in price
body: In 1980s India, Amit Varma recalled, a second-hand car cost more than a new one, because a new car took seven years to be delivered. {096-S09}
A telephone meant a seven-year wait too, and everything was expensive, “even for elite like we were”. The opening up of 1991 changed that.

People normalise such costs, Varma argued, and stop seeing them. Today’s tariffs and non-tariff barriers are just as hidden. Remove them, he said, and cars would be 30 per cent cheaper: the car he bought for ten lakhs would have cost seven. {#cars}

~ Electronics would be cheaper too, and pretty much everything would be cheaper and better. He would do it unilaterally. “All tariffs all countries. That’s good for our people. Think only of our people,” he said.

quote.text: We had normalized that world where a secondhand car would cost more than a new car.

stories.start: We saw newspaper stories of Apple filling up planes to the gills
stories.end: transporting from China to America just made no sense with the new tariffs
stories.caption: Apple’s iPhone airlift
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on supply chains rewired overnight
stories.head: Packed to the gills in Madras
body: As the tariffs on China landed, Ajay Shah said, newspapers reported that Apple was filling planes “to the gills” with iPhones and flying them from Madras to America. {096-S07}
Under the new tariffs, shipping them from China to America made no sense. “This is just all going crazy,” Shah said.

The airlift is one picture of a wider shock. Large companies are looking at their production arrangements and asking what to do, with Donald Trump holding great power till November 2026, and maybe beyond.

~ Supply chains tuned over decades, with a factory in Madras, another in China, another in Argentina and distribution in America, are in disarray. Amit Varma added that uncertainty changes how firms invest, plan and expand.
stories.why: When policy turns on a whim, firms spend effort routing around it instead of producing. Shah likened wrecking the global arrangement to bombing factories: it reduces the world’s capital stock. {096-C12}

stories.start: when Germany was sending leopard two tanks into Ukraine, should Germany continue to sell
stories.end: Now dual use equipment gets you into very messy territory
stories.caption: the Leopard and the T-90
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where trade ends and war begins
stories.head: Tanks to Ukraine, tools to Russia
body: Germany was sending Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine. At the same time, Ajay Shah said, the question arose whether it should go on selling Russia the precision machine tools used to make T-90 tanks on the other side. {096-S03}
“Why would you arm the people who are fighting wars with you?” he asked. Pure free trade became hard to defend, and governments turned to export controls on military and dual-use goods.
Dual-use goods lead into messy territory, he warned, because so much modern high technology overlaps between the consumer world and the military world.
~ Amit Varma framed it as two paradigms, the positive-sum world of trade and the negative-sum world of war. It is not a binary, he said: the two will always coexist. {#paradigm}
stories.why: Once war is real, selling to whoever pays collides with not arming your enemy. In the Second World War America was “the arsenal of democracy”; that capability, Shah said, now sits in China. {096-J17}

quiz.q: What did ‘most favoured nation’ mean in America’s 1934 trade law, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: A tariff cut negotiated with one country is extended to every country.

quiz.q: Why did the GATT’s designers leave agriculture out of the post-war trade club?
quiz.a: To avoid fights with small but lethal farm lobbies, like Japan’s rice farmers.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s imagined negotiation over Ladakh, what does China threaten to cut off?
quiz.a: API exports to India, the raw ingredients its generic drug makers depend on.

quiz.q: How does Amit Varma illustrate why a bilateral trade deficit means nothing?
quiz.a: He runs a deficit with his egg seller, who never buys his podcasting services.

quiz.q: Which levy did India drop on its own when the tariff trouble began?
quiz.a: The 6 per cent equalisation levy, the so-called Google tax.

quiz.q: Why, as Amit Varma remembers the 1980s, did a used car cost more than a new one?
quiz.a: Because a new car then took seven years to be delivered.
